l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and
s: The unit distinguishes the enduring Tao and enduring name from forms that can be trodden or named. The Tao is described as the Originator of heaven and earth when conceived without a name and as the Mother of all things when conceived with a name. It teaches that freedom from desire reveals the deep mystery, while desire reveals only the outer fringe, and that the two aspects together are called the Mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and
s: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. Conceived of as having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; conceived of as having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

l: name, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and
s: The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. Conceived of as having a name, it is associated with the Tao as the Mother of all things.

l: desire, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and
s: When desire is absent, the deep mystery can be sounded. When desire is present, only the outer fringe is seen.

l: Mystery, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and
s: The two aspects of the Tao are really the same, though they receive different names as development takes place. Together they are called the Mystery, and where it is deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 2. 1. All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing
s: The unit explains how opposites and contrasts give rise to one another, including existence and non-existence, difficulty and ease, and length and shortness. It states that the sage manages affairs without doing anything and conveys instructions without speech. All things arise, grow, undergo their processes, and complete their work without claiming ownership or expecting reward. The work is done invisibly, and this is why the power does not cease.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: The unit concerns how the sage should govern the people. It says that not valuing and employing men of superior ability prevents rivalry, while not displaying desirable or difficult-to-procure things prevents theft and disorder. The sage empties the people's minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones. He keeps them without knowledge and desires, restrains those with knowledge from acting on it, and thereby establishes universal good order.

s: The people are kept from rivalry, theft, and disorder through the sage's governance. The sage empties their minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones.

s: Not showing the people what is likely to excite their desires is presented as a way to keep their minds from disorder. The sage constantly tries to keep the people without desire.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: The sage exercises government by emptying the people's minds, filling their bellies, weakening their wills, and strengthening their bones. He keeps them without knowledge and desire and prevents those with knowledge from presuming to act on it.

l: government, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: In the exercise of government, the sage uses abstinence from action and disciplines the conditions of the people to produce good order.

l: knowledge, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: The sage constantly tries to keep the people without knowledge. When there are those who have knowledge, he keeps them from presuming to act on it.

l: action, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: The sage restrains those with knowledge from presuming to act on it. When there is abstinence from action, good order is universal.

l: good order, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
s: Good order is universal when there is abstinence from action.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 4. 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our
s: The unit describes the Tao as like the emptiness of a vessel, warning people to guard against fullness when employing it. It presents the Tao as deep, unfathomable, pure, and still, possibly the Honoured Ancestor of all things. It advises people to blunt sharp points, unravel complications, temper brightness, and agree with others’ obscurity. The Tao’s origin is unknown, though it may have existed before God.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 4. 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our
s: The Tao is compared to the emptiness of a vessel, and people are warned to guard against fullness when employing it. It is described as deep, unfathomable, pure, and still, possibly the Honoured Ancestor of all things. Its origin is unknown, though it might have existed before God.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: Heaven and earth do not act from a wish to be benevolent and deal with all things as dogs of grass are dealt with. The sages likewise do not act from a wish to be benevolent and deal with the people as dogs of grass are dealt with. The space between heaven and earth is compared to a bellows that is emptied without losing its power and produces more air when moved again. Much speech leads to swift exhaustion, so the inner being should be guarded and kept free.

l: Heaven and Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: Heaven and earth do not act from a wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as dogs of grass are dealt with.

l: benevolence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: Benevolence is not the impulse guiding heaven and earth or the sages in how they deal with things or people.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: All things are dealt with by heaven and earth as dogs of grass are dealt with.

l: dogs of grass, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: Dogs of grass are used as the comparison for how heaven and earth deal with all things and how the sages deal with the people.

l: sages, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: The sages do not act from a wish to be benevolent; they deal with the people as dogs of grass are dealt with.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: The people are dealt with by the sages as dogs of grass are dealt with.

l: space between heaven and earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: The space between heaven and earth is compared to a bellows.

l: bellows, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: A bellows is emptied without losing its power, and when moved again it sends forth more air.

l: inner being, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 5. 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be
s: The inner being should be guarded and kept free because much speech leads to swift exhaustion.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 6.
s: The unit concerns the valley spirit and the female mystery. It says that the valley spirit does not die and remains unchanged. The female mystery is identified with the gate from which beings first issued forth, called the root from which heaven and earth grew. Its power remains long and unbroken when used gently and without pain.

l: valley spirit, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 6.
s: The valley spirit does not die and remains always the same. Its power remains long and unbroken when used gently and without the touch of pain.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 7. 1. Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long. The reason
s: The unit concerns Heaven, earth, and the sage. Heaven and earth endure for a long time because they do not live for themselves. The sage places his own person last and treats it as foreign, yet his person is preserved and he attains his private ends. The text presents the lack of personal and private ends as the reason such ends are realised.

l: Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 7. 1. Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long. The reason
s: Heaven is long-enduring because it does not live of or for itself.

l: Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 7. 1. Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long. The reason
s: Earth continues for a long time because it does not live of or for itself.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 7. 1. Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long. The reason
s: The sage puts his own person last and treats it as foreign, yet his person is preserved. Because he has no personal and private ends, such ends are realised.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence
s: The unit describes the highest excellence through the example of water, which benefits all things and occupies the low place without striving. It also identifies excellence in residence, mind, associations, government, affairs, and movement according to suitability, stillness, virtue, good order, ability, and timeliness. The highest excellence does not wrangle about a low position, so no one finds fault with it.

l: highest excellence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence
s: The highest excellence is like water: it benefits all things and occupies the low place without striving. Its way is near to that of the Tao, and because it does not wrangle about its low position, no one finds fault with it.

l: water, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence
s: Water benefits all things and occupies, without striving, the low place which all men dislike. Its excellence is presented as resembling the highest excellence.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence
s: The way of the highest excellence is said to be near to that of the Tao.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: The unit concerns the proper limits of use, possession, achievement, and recognition. It says that an unfilled vessel is better than one carried when full, and that repeatedly feeling a sharpened point causes it to lose its sharpness. Gold, jade, wealth, and honours cannot be kept safely when they fill a hall or produce arrogance. After work is completed and a name becomes distinguished, withdrawing into obscurity is presented as the way of Heaven.

l: vessel, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: A vessel is better left unfilled than carried when it is full.

l: wealth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: When wealth leads to arrogance, it brings evil on itself.

l: honours, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: When honours lead to arrogance, they bring evil on themselves.

l: work, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: When the work is done, withdrawing into obscurity is the way of Heaven.

l: Obscurity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: Withdrawing into obscurity after work is done and one's name becomes distinguished is the way of Heaven.

l: Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 9. 1. It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to
s: Heaven's way is for one to withdraw into obscurity after completing the work and becoming distinguished.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The unit concerns the union of the intelligent and animal souls, disciplined attention to the vital breath, and the cultivation of a flawless state. It discusses loving the people and ruling the state without purposeful action, while intelligence may appear as without knowledge. It describes The Tao as producing and nourishing all things without claiming, boasting, or controlling them, calling this The mysterious Quality.

l: vital breath, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The vital breath receives undivided attention and is brought to the utmost degree of pliancy, allowing one to become as a tender babe.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The people are to be loved without proceeding through purposeful action.

l: state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The state is to be ruled without proceeding through purposeful action.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The Tao produces and nourishes all things, does all without boasting, and presides over all without controlling them.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: All things are produced and nourished by The Tao.

l: The mysterious Quality, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one
s: The mysterious Quality is what The Tao's producing, nourishing, acting without boasting, and presiding without control is called.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: The passage concerns the wheel, vessels, and an apartment, explaining how each depends on empty space for its use. Thirty spokes unite in the wheel’s one nave, while the empty space for the axle makes the wheel useful. Clay vessels and an apartment formed by doors and windows likewise depend on their empty hollowness or interior space, so what exists serves adaptation and what is absent serves usefulness.

l: wheel, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: The wheel has thirty spokes united in one nave, and its use depends on the empty space for the axle.

l: vessels, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: The vessels are fashioned from clay, and their use depends on their empty hollowness.

l: apartment, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: The apartment is formed by cutting out doors and windows from walls, and its use depends on the empty space within.

l: empty space, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: The empty space for the axle, within vessels, and within an apartment enables their use.

l: use, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty
s: Use depends on empty space, while what has positive existence serves for profitable adaptation.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 12.
s: The passage describes how sensory pleasures can overwhelm perception and alter human conduct. Colors, musical notes, flavors, chariot racing, hunting, and rare or strange objects are presented as distractions that deprive the senses and make the mind mad. It teaches that the sage satisfies the craving of the belly rather than the insatiable longing of the eyes. The sage puts aside the latter desire and prefers the former.

l: mind, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 12.
s: The mind is made mad by the chariot course, wild hunting, and rare and strange objects sought for by people.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 12.
s: The sage seeks to satisfy the craving of the belly rather than the insatiable longing of the eyes. The sage puts aside the latter and prefers to seek the former.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: The unit concerns favour, disgrace, honour, great calamity, the body, and the administration of the kingdom. Favour and disgrace are equally feared because gaining favour creates apprehension of losing it, while losing it leads to fear of greater calamity. Honour and great calamity are personal conditions because the body makes a person liable to great calamity. An administrator who honours the kingdom as his own person and loves it as his own person may be entrusted with governing it.

l: favour, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: Favour is equally to be feared with disgrace. Getting favour leads to apprehension of losing it.

l: disgrace, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: Disgrace is being in a low position after the enjoyment of favour. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.

l: honour, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: Honour is to be regarded as a personal condition, similarly to great calamity. He who honours the kingdom as he honours his own person may be employed to govern it.

l: great calamity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: Great calamity is to be regarded as a personal condition. The body makes a person liable to great calamity; without the body, no great calamity could come to that person.

l: body (which I call myself), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: The body is what makes a person liable to great calamity. If the person had not the body, no great calamity could come to the person.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: The kingdom may be entrusted to one who administers it with the love he bears to his own person. It may also be governed by one who honours it as he honours his own person.

l: administrator (of the kingdom), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and
s: An administrator who would administer the kingdom while honouring it as his own person may be employed to govern it. One who administers it with the love he bears to his own person may be entrusted with it.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 14. 1. We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the
s: The text describes the Tao through three qualities: it is not seen, not heard, and not grasped. These qualities cannot be described separately, so they are blended into The One. The Tao is neither bright nor obscure, acts ceaselessly, cannot be named, and returns to nothing. It is encountered without seeing its front or back, and knowing the Tao of old helps direct the present and unravel its clue.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 14. 1. We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the
s: The Tao is described as unseen, unheard, and beyond grasp, with these qualities combined as The One. It has no brightness or obscurity, acts ceaselessly, cannot be named, and returns to nothing. Knowing the Tao as it was of old helps direct the things of the present day and is called unwinding its clue.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: The unit concerns the skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times and their subtle comprehension of the Tao's mysteries. They appeared cautious, irresolute, grave, evanescent, unpretentious, vacant, and dull. It teaches that muddy water becomes clear through stillness, while the condition of rest arises when movement continues. Those who preserve this method of the Tao do not wish to be full of themselves, and therefore can seem worn rather than new and complete.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: The Tao has mysteries comprehended by the skilful masters (of the Tao). Its method is preserved by those who do not wish to be full of themselves.

l: the skilful masters (of the Tao), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times subtly and exquisitely penetrated and comprehended the Tao's mysteries. They appeared cautious, irresolute, grave, evanescent, unpretentious, vacant, and dull.

l: muddy water, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: Muddy water gradually becomes clear when it is allowed to remain still.

l: movement, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: Movement is allowed to go on, and through it the condition of rest gradually arises.
